## Christ references across drafted chapters

- **I AM (ehyeh / YHWH)** — 3:14 (God's self-naming to Moses — ehyeh asher ehyeh, ‘I AM THAT I AM’ — anchors the LORD's covenant name YHWH (Yahweh / Jehovah). Jesus' ‘Before Abraham was, I am’ (John 8:58) and the seven ‘I am’ predicates of John's Gospel deliberately invoke this self-disclosure. Latter-day Saint theology identifies Jehovah of the OT with the pre-mortal Jesus Christ.)
- **Angel of the LORD (malak YHWH)** — 3:2 (‘The angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush’ (3:2); subsequent verses (3:4-6) name the speaker as the LORD / God Himself. The malak YHWH passages of the OT — here, Gen 16, 22, 31 — are read in Christian and Latter-day Saint tradition as Christophanies (visible appearances of the pre-incarnate Word/Son).)

## Per-chapter highlights

### Chapter 1 — Israel Oppressed in Egypt

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, faith, judgment

Genesis 50 ended with a coffin in Egypt and a promise of return; Exodus 1 opens four centuries later, with the seventy grown into a people that fills the land and a new king who knew not Joseph rising to crush them. Three stages of oppression follow — forced labor, an order to the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah, then a command to drown every newborn son in the Nile. The midwives fear God and do not as the king has said; the chapter ends with Pharaoh's order standing and the people still multiplying.

### Chapter 2 — Moses' Birth, Flight, and Marriage

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, faith, restoration

A Levite couple hides their newborn son three months, then places him in a small ark of bulrushes among the reeds of the Nile — turning Pharaoh's drowning-decree back on itself. Pharaoh's daughter draws him out, names him Moses, and his own mother nurses him for hire. Grown, Moses kills an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, flees to Midian, helps the priest's daughters at a well, marries Zipporah, and names his firstborn Gershom — "a stranger there." Pharaoh dies; God hears Israel's groaning and remembers His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

### Chapter 3 — The Burning Bush; the Divine Name

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, divine-name, messianic-prophecy, faith

Moses leads his father-in-law's flock to Horeb, the mountain of God. The angel of the LORD appears to him in a bush that burns without being consumed; God calls "Moses, Moses," names the ground holy, identifies Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and announces that He has come down to deliver Israel. When Moses asks God's name to bring to the elders, God answers: ehyeh asher ehyeh — "I AM THAT I AM" — and names Himself YHWH, the LORD, "this is my name for ever, and this is my memorial unto all generations."

### Chapter 4 — Moses' Objections; the Signs; the Return

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, faith

Moses' remaining objections are answered: three signs (rod-to-serpent, leprous-then-clean hand, water-to-blood), the question "Who hath made man's mouth?", and at last in anger the appointment of Aaron as spokesman. Moses returns to Egypt; the LORD declares Israel His firstborn son, and an opaque night incident at a lodging-place is resolved by Zipporah's circumcising her son. Aaron meets Moses, the elders are gathered, the signs are given; the people believe and worship.

### Chapter 5 — Brick Without Straw

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, faith, prophetic-call

Moses and Aaron deliver the LORD's demand to Pharaoh — "Let my people go" — and meet the OT's first verbalized rejection of the divine name: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?" Pharaoh retaliates by removing the straw from the Israelites' brick quota while leaving the quota itself unchanged; the Hebrew officers are beaten when the tally falls short, and turn on Moses and Aaron with the chapter's closing reproach. Moses returns to the LORD with the OT's most direct prophetic complaint: "Wherefore hast thou so evil entreated this people? why is it that thou hast sent me?"

### Chapter 6 — I Am the LORD; the Levitical Genealogy

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, divine-name, faith, prophetic-call

The LORD answers Moses' end-of-Exodus-5 protest with the covenant declaration bracketed by "I am the LORD" — a four-fold promise to bring out, rid, redeem, and take Israel to be His people — and discloses that the patriarchs had known God as El Shaddai but had not yet experienced Him under the redemptive name Jehovah. The people do not hearken for anguish of spirit, and Moses again pleads "uncircumcised lips." The chapter closes with a tightly focused Levitical genealogy positioning Aaron and Moses within the priestly line.

### Chapter 7 — Aaron's Rod and the Plague of Blood

*status:* draft
*themes:* judgment, covenant, prophetic-call

The plagues narrative opens — Moses set as a divine voice to Pharaoh with Aaron as prophet; the rod-to-serpent sign before Pharaoh matched by the Egyptian magicians' enchantments but Aaron's serpent swallows theirs. The first plague follows: the Nile and all the waters of Egypt are turned to blood, the fish die, the river stinks, and the Egyptians dig for water beside their dying river. The magicians replicate on a small scale; Pharaoh hardens his heart and the chapter records the seven-day duration of the first blow.

### Chapter 8 — Frogs, Lice, and Flies

*status:* draft
*themes:* judgment, covenant

Three plagues in sequence — frogs covering Egypt and dying in heaps, lice rising from the dust at which the Egyptian magicians fail and confess "This is the finger of God," and swarms of flies from which Goshen is for the first time spared by divine division between peoples. Pharaoh begins to bargain — calling for Moses, promising release, hardening his heart once the relief comes. The chapter introduces the plague-cycle's recurring shape: announcement, blow, partial concession under pressure, broken word once the pressure lifts.

### Chapter 9 — Murrain, Boils, and Hail

*status:* draft
*themes:* judgment, covenant

Three plagues in escalating severity — the murrain killing Egypt's livestock while sparing Israel's, the boils that strike the Egyptian magicians and prevent their standing before Moses, and the thunder-and-hail mingled with fire that smites every man, beast, and herb left in the field. The chapter contains the plagues narrative's longest declaration of divine purpose (Exod 9:16, which Paul quotes at Rom 9:17), the first fear-of-the-LORD among Pharaoh's servants, and Pharaoh's first confession of sin — promptly withdrawn once the storm ceases.

### Chapter 10 — Locusts and Darkness

*status:* draft
*themes:* judgment, covenant

The eighth and ninth plagues, framed by the chapter's catechetical statement of purpose: that fathers might tell their sons what the LORD has done. An east wind brings locusts that cover the land and consume what the hail had left; a thick darkness then falls for three days, while Israel has light. Pharaoh's servants break with their king for the first time ("knowest thou not yet that Egypt is destroyed?"); Pharaoh's escalating concessions are all refused; the audience ends with Pharaoh's threat ("see my face no more") and Moses' reply that he will not seek it again.

### Chapter 11 — The Final Plague Announced

*status:* draft
*themes:* judgment, covenant, prophetic-call

The LORD announces one final plague. In their last audience Moses warns Pharaoh: at midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die — from the throne-heir to the maidservant's child to the firstborn of beasts — while not a dog moves its tongue against Israel. The people are instructed to ask jewels of silver and gold from their Egyptian neighbors (the four-century Abrahamic promise of going out with great substance now being kept), and Moses leaves Pharaoh in great anger.

### Chapter 12 — Passover Instituted; the Firstborn Slain

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, messianic-prophecy, judgment, restoration, faith

The Passover is instituted: an unblemished male lamb of the first year, kept from the tenth to the fourteenth day, killed at evening, its blood struck on the doorposts and lintel, its flesh eaten roast with unleavened bread and bitter herbs in haste. At midnight the LORD slays every Egyptian firstborn while passing over every blood-marked house; Pharaoh sends Israel out; six hundred thousand men on foot, plus a mixed multitude, go up from Rameses to Succoth at the close of four hundred and thirty years' sojourn. The Passover ordinance is made permanent — a memorial throughout all generations.

### Chapter 13 — Firstborn Consecrated; the Pillar of Cloud and Fire

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration, faith, messianic-prophecy

Israel's firstborn are consecrated to the LORD ("whatsoever openeth the womb"), with a sign on the hand and frontlets between the eyes established as perpetual memorial, the unleavened-bread feast reaffirmed, and the father-to-son catechetical pattern returned. Moses takes Joseph's bones in fulfillment of the four-century-old oath. The LORD leads Israel not by the direct Philistine road but through the wilderness, going before them in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.

### Chapter 14 — The Crossing of the Red Sea

*status:* draft
*themes:* faith, judgment, restoration, covenant

Pharaoh's hardened heart pursues; the chariots overtake Israel at the sea; the terrified people accuse Moses of bringing them to die in the wilderness, and Moses answers with the OT's foundational word on faith under pursuit: "Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD." A strong east wind divides the sea all night; Israel walks through on dry ground; the morning waters return and overwhelm Pharaoh's army. The chapter closes with Israel seeing the great work, fearing the LORD, and believing both the LORD and His servant Moses.

### Chapter 15 — The Song of Moses and Miriam; the Bitter Waters

*status:* draft
*themes:* faith, covenant, restoration

The Song of Moses (15:1-18) — one of the OT's earliest and most archaic Hebrew compositions — celebrates the deliverance through imagery of the LORD's right hand, the depths covering Pharaoh's army, and the LORD's eternal reign. Miriam answers with timbrel and dance; the women sing the song's opening refrain. Three days into the wilderness, at Marah, the people murmur over bitter waters; the LORD shows Moses a tree to sweeten them and gives the first wilderness statute: "I am the LORD that healeth thee."

### Chapter 16 — Manna and Quail

*status:* draft
*themes:* faith, covenant, restoration

The whole congregation murmurs against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness of Sin, missing Egypt's flesh-pots; the LORD answers with quail at evening and "bread from heaven" at morning. Manna falls daily, one omer per person; the double portion on the sixth day honors the seventh-day sabbath rest before Sinai legislates it. Israel's testing is whether they will trust the daily provision; an omer is laid up before the Testimony as a generational memorial.

### Chapter 17 — Water from the Rock; Amalek Defeated

*status:* draft
*themes:* faith, judgment, covenant, messianic-prophecy

At Rephidim there is no water and the people chide Moses, who names the place Massah ("testing") and Meribah ("strife"); the LORD has Moses smite the rock at Horeb and water comes out. Amalek attacks and Joshua leads the men, while Moses stands on the hill with the rod of God lifted and his hands held up by Aaron and Hur — Israel prevails. Moses builds an altar and names it Jehovah-nissi, "the LORD my banner."

### Chapter 18 — Jethro's Visit; the Appointment of Judges

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, faith, prophetic-call

Jethro, Moses' Midianite father-in-law and priest of Midian, brings Zipporah and Moses' two sons back to Israel at the mount of God, hears the deliverance recounted, and confesses that the LORD is greater than all gods. Watching Moses judge the people single- handedly from morning to evening, Jethro counsels delegation: able men set as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, with only the great matters brought to Moses. Moses accepts the counsel and implements the structure.

### Chapter 19 — Arrival at Sinai; the Third-Day Theophany

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, messianic-prophecy, divine-name, faith

Israel reaches the wilderness of Sinai in the third month and camps before the mount, where the LORD's covenant proposal is delivered through Moses: if Israel obeys His voice, they will be "a peculiar treasure... a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation." The people agree; consecration is appointed for three days; bounds are set around the mount. On the third day the mount shakes, thunders and lightnings and thick cloud descend, the trumpet sounds exceeding loud, smoke ascends as from a furnace, and Moses ascends to meet the LORD.

### Chapter 20 — The Ten Commandments

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, prophetic-call, divine-name

The Decalogue — Hebrew aseret hadevarim, "the ten words" — is given in the Sinai theophany's thunder, the LORD speaking from the mount "all these words" directly to the people. The covenant-prologue ("I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt") grounds the commandments in redemptive history. The people, trembling, ask Moses to speak with God for them; Moses draws near the thick darkness while the people stand afar off, and the LORD continues with altar-instruction that opens the Book of the Covenant.

### Chapter 21 — The Book of the Covenant Opens: Laws on Servants and Persons

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, restoration

The Book of the Covenant (Exod 20:22-23:33) opens with case-law on Hebrew servants (six-year service then release in the seventh, with voluntary lifetime-service marked by piercing the ear at the doorpost), on capital offenses (murder, kidnapping, striking or cursing one's parents), on personal injury (the lex talionis ‘life for life, eye for eye’ as judicial proportionality), on injury to a woman with child, and on the goring ox's owner-liability framework that becomes the OT's foundational text on culpable negligence.

### Chapter 22 — Property, Restitution, and Social Ethics

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, restoration

The Book of the Covenant continues with property-restitution law (four- or five-fold for slaughtered theft; double for recovered; protection against the surprised-thief and inflated claims), shifts through fire and bailment liability and into seduction law, then pivots to the chapter's most distinctive material: the sojourner, widow, and fatherless are not to be vexed or oppressed; usury to the poor is forbidden; the pledged garment must be returned by sundown — "for I am gracious."

### Chapter 23 — Justice, Sabbaths, Feasts, and the Angel Sent Before

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, restoration, messianic-prophecy

The Book of the Covenant closes with judicial-integrity provisions (no false witness, no following a multitude to do evil, no bribe, no oppression of the stranger), the sabbatical-year land-rest and weekly sabbath, and the three pilgrimage feasts (Unleavened Bread, Harvest / Pentecost, Ingathering). The chapter ends with the LORD's promise to send an Angel before Israel "to keep thee in the way" — the Angel in whom "my name is in him" — to drive out the inhabitants of the land little by little.

### Chapter 24 — Covenant Ratified; the Vision on the Mount

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, messianic-prophecy, prophetic-call, faith

The Sinai covenant is formally ratified. Moses reads the Book of the Covenant; the people answer "All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient"; half the sacrificial blood is sprinkled on the altar and half on the people as "the blood of the covenant." Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders go up and see the God of Israel, with a sapphire pavement beneath His feet, and eat and drink in His presence. Moses ascends the mount alone for forty days and nights to receive the tables of stone.

### Chapter 25 — Tabernacle Instructions Begin: Ark, Table, Lampstand

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, messianic-prophecy, restoration, divine-name

The Tabernacle instructions begin. The LORD calls for a freewill offering and gives the foundational purpose: "let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them." The chapter then specifies the three innermost furnishings — the ark of the testimony with its mercy seat and overshadowing cherubim (where the LORD will meet with Moses and commune from above the mercy seat), the table of showbread, and the seven-branched lampstand of pure beaten gold. Each is to be made "after the pattern" shown Moses in the mount.

### Chapter 26 — The Tabernacle Structure: Curtains, Boards, Veil

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, messianic-prophecy, restoration

The Tabernacle's enclosing structure is specified: ten inner curtains of fine twined linen with cherubim worked into them; eleven outer curtains of goats' hair; coverings of dyed ram skins and badgers' skins; the framework of forty-eight upright shittim-wood boards socketed in silver. The veil of blue, purple, and scarlet with cherubim divides the holy place from the most holy — the curtain that the temple-rending at Christ's crucifixion will undo and that Hebrews reads as "his flesh."

### Chapter 27 — The Bronze Altar, the Court, and the Continual Lamp

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, messianic-prophecy

The Tabernacle's outer-court furnishings are specified: the bronze altar of sacrifice (five cubits square, three cubits high, with horns at each corner, of shittim wood overlaid with brass) where burnt offerings are made; the surrounding court enclosed by fine- twined-linen hangings on bronze pillars in silver fillets, 100 cubits by 50 with its gate-screen of blue, purple, and scarlet needlework; and the pure beaten olive oil that keeps the lamp burning continually from evening to morning before the LORD.

### Chapter 28 — Priestly Garments: Ephod, Breastplate, Urim and Thummim

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, messianic-prophecy, prophetic-call

The priestly garments are specified — for Aaron's "glory and beauty" and for ministerial service. The ephod and breastplate of judgment bear the names of Israel's twelve tribes on two onyx shoulder-stones and on twelve breastplate gemstones; the Urim and Thummim go into the breastplate; the robe of the ephod is fringed with bells and pomegranates; the gold plate engraved "HOLINESS TO THE LORD" sits on the high priest's forehead. Aaron bears Israel's names and Israel's iniquity before the LORD continually.

### Chapter 29 — Aaronic Consecration; the Continual Burnt Offering

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, messianic-prophecy, prophetic-call

The consecration ritual for Aaron and his sons is specified: washing at the door of the tent, robing in the priestly garments, anointing with oil, then three sacrifices in sequence — a sin-offering bullock, a burnt-offering ram, and a "ram of consecration" whose blood is applied to the right ear, right thumb, and right great toe of each priest. The chapter then institutes the continual burnt offering of two lambs daily, morning and evening, with its accompanying flour and drink offerings — the perpetual sacrifice that Israel's days will run between for centuries.

### Chapter 30 — Incense Altar, Atonement Money, Laver, Holy Oil, Holy Incense

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, messianic-prophecy, prophetic-call

Five distinct cultic provisions: the gold incense-altar where Aaron burns sweet incense morning and evening before the veil; the half- shekel atonement-money paid alike by rich and poor at every census as a ransom for the soul; the bronze laver between altar and tent for the priests' hand- and foot-washing; the compound anointing oil of myrrh, cinnamon, calamus, cassia, and olive oil that consecrates the Tabernacle and priests; and the compound holy incense of stacte, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense that ascends before the LORD.

### Chapter 31 — Bezalel and Aholiab; the Sabbath as Covenant Sign

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, restoration

The Tabernacle instructions close with two final designations: the LORD calls Bezalel of Judah and Aholiab of Dan by name, filling Bezalel with the Spirit of God in wisdom and craftsmanship for the entire work. The sabbath commandment is restated as the covenant sign between the LORD and Israel — the third great OT covenant sign (after the rainbow at Noah and circumcision at Abraham). The chapter closes the seven-chapter instruction-block with Moses receiving the two tables of testimony, "written with the finger of God."

### Chapter 32 — The Golden Calf; Moses' Intercession

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, judgment, restoration, prophetic-call, messianic-prophecy

The covenant-breach apex of the Pentateuch. While Moses receives the Tabernacle pattern on the mount, the people compel Aaron to make a golden calf and proclaim "These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt." The LORD threatens to consume them; Moses' intercession turns the wrath ("blot me out of thy book"). Moses descends, breaks the tablets, destroys the calf, calls the Levites to the LORD's side and they slay three thousand; Moses returns to the mount to plead atonement for the people's sin.

### Chapter 33 — Show Me Thy Glory; the Cleft of the Rock

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, messianic-prophecy, divine-name

The Golden Calf's fallout. The LORD will send Israel on with an Angel before them but will not Himself go up "in the midst of thee"; the people mourn and strip their ornaments. Moses pitches the tent of meeting outside the camp where the LORD speaks with him "face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend," and his three escalating intercessions climax in "shew me thy glory" — answered by the cleft-of-the-rock passage where Moses sees the LORD's back parts as His glory passes by.

### Chapter 34 — Covenant Renewed; the Second Tables; Moses' Shining Face

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, messianic-prophecy, divine-name, restoration

Moses hews two new stone tablets and ascends Sinai again. The LORD passes by and proclaims the divine-attribute formula — "merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth" — the OT's most-quoted self-revelation of the divine character. The covenant is renewed; Moses' second forty-day fast yields the replacement tables; he descends with face unknowingly shining, wearing a veil except when speaking with the LORD or delivering His word.

### Chapter 35 — Sabbath Reaffirmed; the Freewill Offering Pours In

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration, prophetic-call

Construction of the Tabernacle begins. Moses gathers Israel, reaffirms the sabbath at the construction's threshold, and announces the freewill offering; the response is overwhelming, with every man and woman whose heart stirred them bringing materials and the wise-hearted women spinning the threads. Moses re-presents Bezalel of Judah and Aholiab of Dan, the divinely-named master craftsmen who will lead and teach the work.

### Chapter 36 — Construction Begins: ‘Much More Than Enough’; Curtains, Boards, Veil

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, restoration

The construction is underway. Wise-hearted men work daily; the freewill offerings keep coming "every morning"; finally Moses must order them stopped: "the people bring much more than enough." Bezalel and the craftsmen then begin the Tabernacle proper — the ten linen curtains with cherubim, the eleven goats'-hair curtains, the rams' and badgers' skin coverings, the forty-eight gold-overlaid boards in silver sockets, the cross-bars, the veil of blue, purple, and scarlet with cherubim, and the screen at the tent door.
